newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's new rulers plan free-market social economy.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's new rulers plan free-market social economy.

text.p: Zaire's new leaders mapped out liberal economic policies on Monday but warned its business elite that three decades of corruption and mismanagement under ousted President Mobutu Sese Seko were over.
Two days after Laurent Kabila's rebels marched into the capital Kinshasa, an acting "minister" said the new order's goal was a free-market economy with a human face.
Babi Mbayi, Kabila's adviser on planning and development, held separate meetings with businessmen and heads of the country's notoriously corrupt and ill-run parastatals.
"We are a forgiving government but beneath the velvet glove is steel which resembles a Kalashnikov," he told them.

Kabila, chairman of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire and a former revolutionary Marxist, proclaimed himself president of the newly named Democratic Republic of Congo on Saturday.
He will name his government on Tuesday if he sticks to a self-imposed 72-hour deadline.
Kabila, 56, remained in his provincial headquarters at Lubumbashi and sent a senior Alliance delegation to Kinshasa.

Many of the sleek chairmen of Zaire's parastatals appeared chastened and subdued after a closed-door meeting with Mbayi. None of the former denizens of Mobutu's 32-year regime, once described as a "kleptocracy", was sacked on Monday, it seemed.
"The Alliance told us the first goal was to work with honesty and rigour. We must work in the interests of the people," Leny Elongu, chief executive of state insurance company SONAS, told Reuters.
Mbayi defined the Alliance's policy framework as "a free market social economy" where competition would be encouraged but with rules about fair treatment of employees enshrined in law.
Life has gone downhill for most of Zaire's 40 million people since independence from Belgium in 1960. Decent housing, health care and education are out of reach of the great majority.
"We have won a war but we have another war now, a war for development. We must get to work," Mbayi said.
Mbayi said he had spent 10 years in France and joined the Alliance last November, one month after Kabila launched his rebellion in eastern Zaire.
Keen to get on the right side of the rebels, currency traders in Kinshasa's "Wall Street" area let the battered Zaire currency gain 60 percent against the U.S. dollar on Monday.

Mbayi said an Alliance commission would work on the details of economic and monetary policy. Asked if the new rulers wanted a rate of about 70,000 Zaires to the dollar, in effect on Monday, he told Reuters:
"We shall see. But you cannot impose exchange rates. Our policy is to try to put currency dealers and businessmen together to work out a fair rate," he said.
Business leaders said their main concern was security. Armed men in uniform, believed to be from Mobutu's routed army and security agencies, staged hold-ups and looted on Monday.
The Red Cross said it collected 22 more bodies from Kinshasa's streets on Monday, bringing their number of dead in the violence since Saturday to 222.
Mbayi told the businessmen the Alliance would soon have 10,000 to 20,000 fighters in Kinshasa to ensure security.
